topThreeProblems: Role/company coverage is narrow and single-source: an unfiltered search_defense_roles call returned rolesScanned=200 across only 5 distinct companies (Apex Space, Anduril Industries, Saronic Technologies, Hadrian, Astranis), all pulled from one feed (the a16z speedrun Talent Network) — no defense primes (Lockheed, Northrop, RTX, Palantir, SpaceX) and nothing outside that one network, which caps real-world value for most job-seekers in this space.

PII/CUI protection is keyword/pattern-based, not a general classifier: it correctly caught every one of 6 adversarial payloads I sent (an SSN, a DOB, a passport number, a DCSA case number, and a classification marking, spread across explain_rule, search_defense_roles, verify_evidence, and prepare_consented_card), but an enumerated filter is inherently bypassable by sufficiently obfuscated or out-of-list sensitive data (e.g. a spelled-out number, a home address) that it wasn't built to recognize — a real residual risk even though nothing I actually tried got through.

Concrete, fixable design/polish paper cuts below a Linear/Vercel/Stripe bar: dark-mode primary-button text (white on --accent-9 #418fe1) measures 3.36:1 contrast, under WCAG AA's 4.5:1 normal-text threshold (it only clears the 3:1 large-text/UI floor); the deterministic no-LLM trial-assessment rubric text is repetitive/formulaic by the product's own admission ('a deterministic starting shape'); and there's no robots.txt (the route falls through to the SPA's own 404 shell) or llms.txt.

function.evidence: Hand-ran the full MCP Streamable-HTTP handshake against https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp: initialize returned protocolVersion 2025-06-18 and serverInfo {name:'clearance-lens',version:'0.1.0'} over SSE; tools/list returned all 11 tools with complete input/output JSON Schemas. Then called all 11 tools with real arguments and got well-formed, schema-conformant results every time: search_defense_roles('autonomy') returned live roles (Saronic 'Perception and Autonomy Engineer', Anduril 'Systems Engineering Manager, Mission Autonomy') with stated/inferred requirement tags; estimate_timeline(secret,none) returned 197 days sourced to a named Sept-2026 DCSA/NISPPAC PDF; verify_evidence('torvalds') pulled real current GitHub data (331,717 followers, a repo pushed 2026-11-12 matching 'today'); get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, fit_debrief, prepare_consented_card, build_trial_assessment, run_job_preview, get_company_profile, and explain_rule all returned correct, schema-matching data. Error paths also work: an invalid enum on estimate_timeline returns a clear Zod-style message listing valid options, an unknown role_id returns a friendly fallback ('may have been filled or removed'), a malformed JSON POST body returns JSON-RPC -32700, and an unknown tool name returns -32602. Separately, in the live /try UI (real browser session, not just the API) I typed 'autonomy', toggled 'ITAR only', and got a genuinely different, correctly-filtered result set (Saronic/Anduril, Secret/Top-Secret tags) — confirming the playground isn't a static mock. Deductions: build_trial_assessment's own output discloses its rubric bands are 'a deterministic starting shape... so this works with no LLM key', meaning raw output is less rich than the pitched agent-assisted experience; and I could not personally test the Claude Desktop/ChatGPT/Cursor connector-UI install flows end-to-end, only the underlying protocol all of them share.

trueUserValue.evidence: The regulatory content is genuinely well-researched: explain_rule('itar') cites 22 CFR 120.62/120.63 and 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3) with eCFR/Cornell LII links; estimate_timeline cites a specific DCSA NISPPAC slide deck and explains why its methodology change makes 197 days follow 180/209/183 in prior quarters — more rigor than a quick web search would surface for a layperson. The 'stated' vs 'inferred' labeling on job-requirement signals (e.g. an Anduril posting's clearance level marked 'stated' while its citizenship requirement is marked 'inferred', with the inference's rationale spelled out) is a genuinely useful, differentiated feature most job boards don't offer. The explicit refusal to score/rank/verify-via-DISS is itself valuable positioning in a space that attracts predatory 'clearance verification' and 'AI hiring score' products. But breadth is a real ceiling: an unfiltered search returned rolesScanned=200 across only 5 companies, all from one source (a16z speedrun Talent Network) — nothing from primes or any company outside that network. And the raw tool output's richness depends on an agent elaborating on top of deterministic templates (confirmed via build_trial_assessment's own disclosure), so the standalone API value is lower than the full agent-assisted pitch implies.

aestheticsUx.evidence: Evaluated via the shipped production CSS/HTML (fetched directly) plus a real rendered accessibility tree from an actual browser session (mcp__wal__browser_snapshot) — no pixel-screenshot tool was available in this environment, so I did not view literal rendered pixels at specific widths; that is a methodology limit on this score, not a product claim. Typography: Geist/GeistMono (Vercel's own family), a calc-based type scale, and a 680px prose-width constraint on long-form pages (/privacy, /sources). Color: full Radix-Colors-style 12-step scales (neutral/accent/success/caution/danger) defined for both light and dark themes via .dark class toggling, plus a 4-level elevation system using a '1px border + soft blur' layering (e.g. '0 0 0 1px #0d101414, 0 2px 4px #0d10140a') that is the same technique Linear/Vercel use, not generic box-shadows. Spacing: a disciplined 4px base grid (--spacing:.25rem). Motion: only one keyframe (pulse) sitewide, and @media(prefers-reduced-motion:reduce) correctly collapses all transition/animation durations to .01ms — more thorough than most production sites bother with. Responsiveness: standard Tailwind breakpoints (640/768/1024/1280/1536px) with real verified layout changes (sm:grid-cols-2/3, lg:grid-cols-2/3, lg:w-[240px] sidebar) rather than just text reflow. Accessibility: a working 'Skip to content' link revealed only on focus, a <main id='main-content'> landmark, correct ARIA roles (switch/tab/tablist/tabpanel) confirmed in a live DOM snapshot, meaningful aria-labels ('Toggle dark mode', 'Copy to clipboard', the full literal install command), 22 distinct focus-visible rules using an accent-colored ring that (via :focus-visible, not :focus) only appears for keyboard users, and zoom not disabled in the viewport meta. I computed WCAG contrast on 14 real token pairs pulled from the CSS: 13 passed AA comfortably (light body text 18.76:1, dark body text 16.58:1), and found one genuine miss — white text on --accent-9 (#418fe1) in dark mode is 3.36:1, under the 4.5:1 normal-text AA threshold. The deterministic trial-assessment rubric copy is also mechanically repetitive. These are real, specific, fixable paper cuts on an otherwise disciplined system — not a fundamentally unpolished product — but I can't personally vouch for pixel-level execution at a literal 375px width.

trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: Tested the privacy claims adversarially rather than trusting the docs. Sent {topic:'123-45-6789 is my SSN, am I eligible?'} to explain_rule — got isError:true, 'This looks like it includes a Social Security Number... please remove it.' Sent an SSN-bearing query to search_defense_roles, a DOB string ('DOB 01/02/1990') to verify_evidence, a passport-number string to explain_rule, a DCSA case-number string to explain_rule, and a 'SECRET//NOFORN' classification marking to prepare_consented_card — all 6 were rejected pre-validation with accurate, specific, plain-language messages matching the worked example published at /privacy. Re-ran the SSN test through the live /try UI (not just raw API calls) and it surfaced a graceful 'Edit and try again' recovery state rather than a crash. No tool among the 11 has a score/rank field in its output schema; get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, and fit_debrief each explicitly state 'not a score, a ranking, or a hire/no-hire recommendation'; verify_evidence and get_company_profile explicitly disclaim inferring protected characteristics. get_company_profile('anduril-industries') returned criteria:[] plus an explicit gaps[] explanation rather than inventing a 'culture fit' read. No tool schema accepts file/image/binary input, and prepare_consented_card's own output states 'DISS/NBIS lookups are restricted to Facility Security Officers by design.' Every factual claim I triggered across 11 tools carried a populated sources[] array with specific, dated, verifiable primary-source URLs (eCFR, Cornell LII, a named DCSA/NISPPAC PDF, academic meta-analyses); the /sources page's '47 sources' claim checks out exactly against its own live category-count breakdown (5+25+10+7=47). Short of a 10 because the PII filter is pattern/keyword-based (evident from its specific, consistent per-category wording), so it's a real but bounded guarantee rather than a general classifier — I could not rule out a sufficiently obfuscated bypass from outside, even though nothing I tried got through.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Every page serves HSTS (max-age=63072000; includeSubDomains; preload), X-Frame-Options: DENY, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, and a Permissions-Policy blocking camera/mic/geolocation. The MCP endpoint correctly implements Streamable HTTP: initialize negotiates protocolVersion 2025-06-18 over text/event-stream, a malformed JSON POST body returns proper JSON-RPC {code:-32700,message:'Parse error: Invalid JSON'} at HTTP 400, an unknown tool name returns {code:-32602,message:'Tool does_not_exist not found'}, tool-level failures correctly use result.isError rather than a transport error, a GET on /mcp correctly 405s with an Allow:POST header, and CORS exposes Mcp-Session-Id with access-control-allow-origin:*. Five rapid sequential tools/list calls all returned HTTP 200 in 298-349ms with no throttling or instability. Across roughly 15 tool calls — including ones hitting live third-party APIs (GitHub for verify_evidence, the a16z speedrun Talent Network for search_defense_roles/get_company_profile) — latency ranged 126-773ms, with the single 773ms outlier on the very first/cold call and everything else in the 130-250ms band; zero 500s or timeouts across the whole session. Minor nits keeping this off a 10: there's no real robots.txt (the route falls through to the SPA's own custom 404 shell) or llms.txt, and the CORS preflight advertises GET as an allowed method on /mcp even though the live route 405s on an actual GET — a small inconsistency, not a functional problem.

hardConstraintViolation.detail: No violation found on any of the six items, each tested directly rather than taken on faith. (a) PII/CUI storage/echo/logging/acceptance: sent 6 adversarial payloads (an SSN, a DOB, a passport number, a DCSA case number, a classification marking — repeated across explain_rule, search_defense_roles, verify_evidence, and prepare_consented_card) and every one was rejected pre-validation with an accurate, specific, plain-language message (e.g. 'This looks like it includes a Social Security Number... please remove it'), both via raw MCP calls and through the live /try UI, which showed a graceful 'Edit and try again' recovery state rather than a crash. Residual caveat: the filter reads as pattern/keyword-based rather than a general PII classifier, so a sufficiently obfuscated or out-of-list input could conceivably slip through — I found no actual instance of this, but can't rule it out from outside. (b) DISS/NBIS/DCSA imitation or screenshot requests: none found; no tool schema among the 11 accepts file/image/binary input, and the product's own output explicitly disclaims this capability ('DISS/NBIS lookups are restricted to Facility Security Officers by design'). (c) ITAR-controlled technical data generation: none found; explain_rule is a closed lookup over roughly 13 fixed topics — I sent it 'javelin missile guidance specs' and it correctly returned found:false plus the fixed topic list rather than fabricating anything, because it isn't generative at all. build_trial_assessment and run_job_preview are verifiably scoped to quoting only the public job posting's own text, with an explicit itarSafetyNote, and run_job_preview's 'ITAR moment' scene models refusing to hand over 'the drawing' rather than describing one. (d) hire/no-hire score, ranking, or demographic inference: none found; no output schema among the 11 tools has a score/rank field, and get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, fit_debrief, verify_evidence, and get_company_profile all explicitly and repeatedly disclaim this. (e) unsourced statistic or claim: none found; every factual claim I triggered across 11 tools carried a populated sources[] array with specific, dated, verifiable primary-source URLs, and the /sources page's '47 sources' claim checks out against its own live category-count breakdown. (f) severe accessibility failure blocking a core task: none found; a working skip-link, a labeled landmark, correct ARIA roles, labeled controls, and 13 of 14 sampled WCAG contrast pairs pass AA. I did find one minor, non-blocking contrast shortfall (white-on-accent-9 button text in dark mode at 3.36:1, under the 4.5:1 normal-text AA bar) and could not personally test raw keyboard Tab-order since my available tooling has no 'press Tab' primitive — neither rises to a severe, task-blocking failure.

judges.overallNarrative:
I tested Clearance Lens two ways: as a raw MCP server (hand-rolled Streamable-HTTP JSON-RPC calls to all 11 tools, plus error-path and malformed-input probes) and as a web app (a real browser session against the homepage, the /try playground, and /sources, plus direct reading of the shipped production CSS/HTML for design-system evidence, since no pixel-screenshot tool was available to me in this environment — I'm flagging that limitation up front rather than pretending to have seen literal rendered pixels at specific widths).

What impressed me most is that the safety claims aren't just marketing copy — they held up under direct, adversarial testing. I threw six different PII/CUI patterns (an SSN, a DOB, a passport number, a DCSA case number, a classification marking) at four different tools, and every single one was caught pre-validation with an accurate, specific, non-alarming message, both via the raw protocol and through the live UI (which recovers gracefully with an 'Edit and try again' state, not a crash). I tried to coerce explain_rule into describing 'javelin missile guidance specs' and it correctly came back empty-handed with its fixed topic list, because it's a closed lookup table, not a generative explainer — a structural choice that makes the ITAR-safety claim load-bearing rather than aspirational. No tool can produce a score or ranking, none queries or imitates DISS/NBIS, and every factual claim I triggered came back with a real, dated, checkable primary source.

As a product designer who's spent time in Linear's, Vercel's, and Stripe's own products: the design system here is unmistakably built with real discipline, not a hackathon template. Geist/Geist Mono, a full Radix-Colors-style 12-step semantic palette in both themes, a layered elevation system, a 4px spacing grid, standard breakpoints with verified real layout changes, and prefers-reduced-motion actually honored sitewide. I computed contrast on 14 real token pairs and 13 passed WCAG AA comfortably — the one genuine miss (white text on the dark-mode accent-9 button fill, 3.36:1) is exactly the kind of specific thing a Linear/Vercel design review would flag and fix in an afternoon, not evidence of a deeper problem.

Where it falls short of 'exceptional': the underlying job-data corpus is narrow (one source, ~200 roles, five companies in practice — Anduril, Saronic, Apex Space, Hadrian, Astranis — nothing from a defense prime or outside that one network), which caps real-world value for a lot of the audience this is pitched at. And some of the raw, no-LLM tool output is explicitly a 'deterministic starting shape' rather than fully polished — the product is honest about this, but it means the standalone API undersells the full agent-assisted experience.

Net assessment: an unusually well-engineered, honestly-scoped, and genuinely safety-conscious product for a narrow slice of the job market — the engineering and trust posture would not embarrass a much bigger team, even if the data breadth and a few design details keep it short of best-in-class.

function.evidence: Ran a real MCP Streamable HTTP session against https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp: initialize (protocolVersion 2025-06-18) succeeded with no session ID required (matches the 'stateless' claim), notifications/initialized returned 202, and tools/list returned all 11 documented tools with matching JSON schemas. resources/list and prompts/list (advertised capabilities) are genuinely populated, not vestigial: 3 real resources (clearance-lens://rules.json, timelines.json, disclaimers.json) and 3 real guided prompts (check_my_eligibility, prep_for_role, preview_the_job). Called all 11 tools with real arguments: search_defense_roles found a live role, 'Manufacturing Test Engineer, Fury' at Anduril (id ca37f753-40c5-7181-c25c-8527f9d46a25); get_role_rubric, estimate_timeline, explain_rule, readiness_brief, build_trial_assessment, run_job_preview, fit_debrief, prepare_consented_card, get_company_profile (anduril-industries), and verify_evidence (github octocat, matched real public GitHub data: followers 25078, created 2011-01-25) all returned well-formed, schema-conformant JSON every time. Confirmed the /try playground is not a separate mock: clicked 'Explain a rule' in a real browser session, typed 'itar', submitted, and got the identical text and the same 3 citation links as the raw MCP call. Deducted for two real gaps: explain_rule's topic lookup missed 'green_card', 'lpr', and 'permanent resident clearance' (exact-keyword matching, not semantic), and search_defense_roles disclosed via its own 'note' field that an itar_only+secret query which reported rolesScanned:200 had only checked requirement signals on the first 25.

trueUserValue.evidence: explain_rule(topic:'itar') gave a correct, primary-source-cited answer to the persona's actual question: under 22 CFR 120.62 a lawful permanent resident (green card holder) IS an ITAR 'U.S. person', with no naturalization-timing condition on that prong, cited to eCFR 120.62/120.63 and 8 U.S.C. 1324b(a)(3) with lastVerified:2026-11-11 -- this is more precise and better-sourced than the contradictory advice the persona describes finding online. run_job_preview's 'ITAR moment' scene (declining to hand a contractor a drawing) and readiness_brief's suggested recruiter question ('Can you confirm exactly what citizenship/US-person status this specific role requires, beyond what's in the posting?') show real awareness of the practical issue. However, across explain_rule('itar'), explain_rule('sead4'), get_role_rubric, and estimate_timeline, the product never surfaces that actual DoD/NISPOM clearance-GRANT eligibility for non-citizens is a separate, much stricter regime (Limited Access Authorizations, Secret/Confidential only, contingent on the employer certifying no U.S. citizen is available) from ITAR's U.S.-person test -- even though 32 CFR 117.10 is cited as a source in estimate_timeline's own sources[]. estimate_timeline's input schema (target_level/current_status/employer_has_fcl) has no citizenship field at all, so it literally cannot give this persona a different, more cautious answer than it would give a citizen. A user could walk away believing the clearance process is just a timeline question once ITAR 'U.S. person' status is confirmed, when in practice very few employers pursue LAAs for a given opening. That gap, on exactly the question this persona most needs answered, caps the value beyond what a good FSO or attorney would say immediately.

aestheticsUx.evidence: Verified hands-on via real browser automation (mcp__wal__browser_snapshot/browser_act) on /try: built on Radix UI with correct ARIA roles (tablist/tab/tabpanel/switch), a 'Skip to content' link, a working dark-mode toggle, 11 clearly labeled tool tabs matching the 11 MCP tools, and role cards in the default 'Search roles' view visibly tagged with stated-vs-inferred badges ('Secret', 'US person required', 'Likely US-person required', 'Clearance possibly required') -- a concrete, visible instantiation of the README's stated/inferred promise. Submitted an SSN through the live UI (typed into the 'Rule topic' field and clicked 'Explain') and got a graceful degraded state with an 'Edit and try again' recovery button rather than a crash or raw error dump. Could not verify true pixel-level polish -- color contrast ratios, spacing/typography refinement, actual mobile-viewport behavior -- because no screenshot or visual-diff capability was available to me, only structural/accessibility-tree snapshots. Score reflects strong, verified structural and interaction design, held below 8+ because I cannot personally confirm the visual craft that would justify a higher mark.

trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: Independently reproduced the /privacy page's own worked SSN example as a live MCP tools/call (not the REST shape it documents) -- POST explain_rule{topic:'123-45-6789 is my SSN, am I eligible?'} returned isError:true with 'This looks like it includes a Social Security Number... please remove it' and did NOT echo the actual digits back. Combined two PII/CUI categories in one request (topic:'I was born 01/02/1990, SECRET//NOFORN access, am I eligible?') and got a correctly itemized rejection of both the DOB pattern and the classification marking in one friendly message. Triggered the 'structured too deeply' guard with a hand-built 60-level-deep nested JSON object in place of a string field and got the exact documented depth-rejection message. Triggered the SSN filter a third way by putting '123-45-6789' in an undeclared field (ssn) inside prepare_consented_card's fields_user_approved, showing the scanner runs independent of schema validation. Reproduced the SSN rejection a fourth time inside the live browser-driven /try UI. Every one of the ~15 substantive tool responses I captured carried sources[] with real primary-source URLs (eCFR, Cornell LII, DCSA/NISPPAC PDF, SEAD 4 PDF, GitHub) and lastVerified:2026-11-11 dates, and every tool that could tempt a score/ranking/demographic read (get_role_rubric, fit_debrief, readiness_brief, get_company_profile, verify_evidence) carried an explicit disclaimer against doing so, matching the actual non-numeric, template-only output received. build_trial_assessment unprompted disclosed 'these bands are a deterministic starting shape (so this works with no LLM key in the /try playground)', structurally confirming no server-side LLM ever sees the user's private answers. Not a 10: I verified the claims only for the specific inputs I tried, not all 47 listed sources, and the topic-matching looseness (see problems list) sits adjacent to full compliance completeness.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Confirmed spec-correct MCP Streamable HTTP behavior: SSE framing (event: message / data: {...}) on list/complex calls, plain application/json on short calls per content negotiation, correct 202 Accepted with empty body on notifications/initialized, no Mcp-Session-Id required anywhere (consistent stateless design). Every response carried strong security headers: strict-transport-security max-age=63072000, x-frame-options: DENY, x-content-type-options: nosniff, permissions-policy blocking camera/microphone/geolocation, and access-control-allow-origin: * appropriate for a public no-auth API. Measured latency directly via curl -w time_total across ~25 calls: 0.28s-1.1s, no timeouts, no 5xx. Deliberately tried to break it: unknown tool name -> clean JSON-RPC -32602 'Tool nonexistent_tool not found'; missing required field, invalid enum, out-of-range limit (999 vs max 25) -> clear Zod-style messages naming the exact field and constraint; nonexistent role_id -> friendly text suggesting re-search rather than a crash; every PII/nesting/schema adversarial input (see trust dimension) -> clean isError:true text, never a stack trace. resources/list and prompts/list are real and substantive, not placeholder capability flags. Not a 10: I could not observe concurrency/load behavior or the actual source, and the search-signal-checking cap (25-of-200, disclosed only in a prose 'note' field) is a real, if honestly disclosed, completeness shortcut.

hardConstraintViolation.detail: (a) PII/CUI stored, echoed, logged, or accepted without rejection -- NOT FOUND. Directly tested SSN, date-of-birth, and classification-marking patterns (individually and combined) through three different entry points -- a raw MCP tools/call to explain_rule, an undeclared field inside prepare_consented_card's fields_user_approved, and the live /try browser UI -- and every single one was rejected (isError:true) with a plain-language explanation that named the category but never echoed the actual sensitive value back. (b) Server queried or imitated DISS/NBIS/DCSA, or asked for a clearance screenshot -- NOT FOUND. No tool's input schema has any field that could carry a screenshot/image or a case/record number; verify_evidence only calls GitHub's public REST API (confirmed by matching octocat's real public data); the privacy page's claim that 'Clearance Lens cannot verify clearance status and never will' is architecturally true given the tool surface I exercised, and this exact sentence is also centrally stored in the disclaimers.json MCP resource. (c) Tool generated or requested ITAR-controlled technical data/drawings/specs -- NOT FOUND. build_trial_assessment and run_job_preview both carry explicit itarSafetyNote/outOfScope fields refusing this, and in practice the content I received (a manufacturing-test-engineer work sample; a 4-scene job preview including an 'ITAR moment' scene) was entirely behavioral/narrative, traced only to quoted public posting text -- the ITAR scene models DECLINING to share a drawing, never generates one. (d) Hire/no-hire score, ranking of people, or demographic inference -- NOT FOUND. No tool accepts more than one candidate's data at all (ranking people is structurally impossible), and get_role_rubric, fit_debrief, readiness_brief, get_company_profile, and verify_evidence all returned qualitative aligned/mixed/unclear template language with an explicit 'never a score, ranking, or hire/no-hire recommendation' / 'never infers protected characteristics' disclaimer, matching the actual output. (e) Any statistic or claim with no source -- NOT FOUND in what I tested. Every numeric or factual claim I received (the 197-day Secret-clearance timeline, the SEAD 4 guideline list, the ITAR U.S.-person definition, DCSA quarter-over-quarter figures) carried a sources[] array with a real primary-source URL and a lastVerified:2026-11-11 date; this is not an exhaustive audit of all 47 listed sources, only of the claims I actually queried. (f) Severe accessibility failure blocking a core task -- NOT FOUND, with a caveat. Using only click/type browser actions I completed the core task end-to-end (searched roles, submitted a rule question, triggered and recovered from a PII rejection via an 'Edit and try again' button), and the page exposes correct ARIA roles (tablist/tab/tabpanel/switch) and a skip-to-content link. I had no pixel-level screenshot or contrast-measurement tool available, so this is a structural/interaction-level accessibility check, not a full WCAG visual audit.

judges.overallNarrative: As a green-card holder trying to get a straight answer on one specific question -- does my immigration status block me from an Anduril Fury role that mentions a Secret clearance -- I connected directly to the live MCP endpoint with raw JSON-RPC calls and also drove the /try playground in a real browser, rather than just reading the README. The single most useful thing I got was explain_rule('itar'): a correctly-sourced statement that a green card holder IS an ITAR 'U.S. person' under 22 CFR 120.62, with citations I could click through to eCFR myself. That alone is better than the scattered, contradictory advice I'd find on forums. The search, rubric, timeline, trial-assessment, and job-preview tools all worked, pulled real live postings, and consistently refused to give me a score or rank -- exactly as advertised. I threw real adversarial input at it too (an SSN, a fake DOB plus a classification marking, a 60-level-deep JSON payload, an undeclared field smuggling an SSN) and it rejected every one of them cleanly, in both the API and the browser UI, matching its own privacy page word for word. Where it fell short for my specific situation: nobody ever told me that actually getting a DoD clearance as a non-citizen is governed by a much stricter, separate rule (Limited Access Authorizations) than the ITAR 'U.S. person' test it did explain -- I'd still need to go read 32 CFR 117.10 myself (which the product cites but never unpacks) or ask an FSO before I'd feel fully informed. I'd add this to my agent for the sourced legal explanations and the realistic job preview, and I'd trust its privacy behavior completely having verified it myself -- but I wouldn't treat its eligibility read as the final word on my own citizenship question.
topThreeProblems: The single most decision-relevant fact for a green-card holder is never surfaced by any tool: DoD/NISPOM clearance *eligibility* for non-citizens (Limited Access Authorizations -- Secret/Confidential only, contingent on the employer certifying no U.S. citizen is available, never granted for TS/SCI/NATO/COMSEC/RD) is a separate, far stricter regime than ITAR's 'U.S. person' test. explain_rule('itar') correctly says LPRs are ITAR U.S. persons, which risks implying equal footing with citizens for the clearance itself, and estimate_timeline's input schema has no citizenship field at all, so it can't even implicitly flag the distinction -- even though 32 CFR 117.10 (the regulation that contains this exact carve-out) is already sitting in estimate_timeline's own sources[] unexplained.

explain_rule's topic lookup is literal keyword matching, not semantic: topic values 'green_card', 'lpr', and 'permanent resident clearance' all returned found:false, even though the itar-us-person topic's own summary directly answers them. It recovers gracefully by returning the full topic list on a miss, so it is friction rather than a dead end, but it means the natural phrasing a user or an LLM agent would try first is likely to fail.

search_defense_roles's exhaustiveness is easy to overstate from its own output: a call with itar_only:true and clearance:'secret' reported rolesScanned:200, but its own 'note' field disclosed that only the first 25 of those 200 postings were actually checked for requirement signals -- a caller that reads the headline count rather than the prose note could wrongly conclude the search covered all 200.

No recruiter-facing surface exists anywhere in the product: every tool is candidate-initiated and one-directional (search, evaluate, build a card, preview a job). There is no way for a recruiter to receive, collect, or compare candidates' readiness briefs, trial-assessment submissions, or consented cards through Clearance Lens itself — a candidate would have to manually paste/email the markdown output. As the recruiter in this lens, that caps how much actual interview-loop time this saves ME versus how much it helps the candidate self-screen before ever reaching me.

Role/company data depends entirely on one upstream source (the a16z speedrun Talent Network). get_company_profile('anduril-industries') returned an empty criteria[] array (no sourced hiring criteria found) and a workRealities.workplaceMix that was 2559/2586 'unspecified' — real coverage gaps the tool discloses honestly rather than hiding, but which mean a company not listed on that network (very plausibly my own early-stage startup) has zero footprint in these tools at all.

Generated deliverables quote source text completely verbatim with no cleanup, including an apparent typo copied straight into an official trial-assessment rubric criterion ('Mange the Anduril Group 5 Mission Autonomy Systems Engineering homeroom', from build_trial_assessment). This is a defensible anti-fabrication design choice, but it means I could not hand a generated rubric or brief directly to a candidate without personally reviewing and cleaning it first, which quietly erodes some of the time-savings pitch.

function.evidence: I spoke raw MCP JSON-RPC (Streamable HTTP) directly against https://clearance-lens.vercel.app/mcp rather than only reading about it. initialize returned a correct handshake (protocolVersion 2024-11-05, capabilities, serverInfo clearance-lens/0.1.0); GET correctly 405'd with a proper JSON-RPC error. tools/list returned exactly the 11 documented tools with full input/output JSON Schemas and readOnlyHint:true annotations. I then called all 11 tools end to end with real arguments (search_defense_roles, explain_rule, estimate_timeline, get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, build_trial_assessment, run_job_preview, fit_debrief, get_company_profile, verify_evidence, prepare_consented_card) and every single one returned well-formed, schema-matching JSON. Error handling was uniformly graceful under adversarial input: invalid enum (minutes:45) -> clear validation message, missing required field (topic) -> clear validation message, unknown tool name -> proper JSON-RPC error, bogus role_id -> a helpful 'couldn't find a role, search again' message rather than a crash. resources/list and prompts/list (not mentioned in the README) also work, exposing the underlying rules/timelines/disclaimers datasets and three ready-made prompts. Latency was consistently 330-460ms across repeated calls. The /try playground rendered real, live data (Anduril/Saronic postings) matching what the direct API returned. Docked from 9-10 because I validated the protocol via raw HTTP/curl rather than a literal connected agent client (Claude Desktop/Cursor), and because of small nits: the 'tool not found' error uses code -32602 rather than the more conventional -32601, and /robots.txt 404s instead of resolving.

trueUserValue.evidence: From the specific lens of a pre-FCL founder/recruiter: estimate_timeline gave a genuinely useful, dated, methodology-aware answer (197-day average Secret clearance, broken into 21/59/117-day phases, plus a separate 3-9 month (6-18 with FOCI) FCL-sponsorship caveat) — more rigorous than what a quick search turns up. explain_rule('itar') correctly distinguished green-card holders from H-1B/O-1/visa holders under 22 CFR 120.62/120.63, exactly the kind of mistake an early-stage non-legal team makes. build_trial_assessment and run_job_preview are the most differentiated tools for this persona: a rubric traceable to quoted posting language (grounded in Sackett et al. 2022) and a 4-scene realistic job preview whose 'ITAR moment' scene correctly models declining to hand controlled data to a non-US-person contractor — this is real reduce-mismatch value a scrappy startup wouldn't build itself. prepare_consented_card worked exactly as advertised (built a clean card from only the fields I supplied, explicitly flagged clearance/citizenship as self-reported/unverified, linked to the real apply URL rather than auto-applying) but its value to ME as recruiter is modest: it's a nicely-formatted self-report, not a verification shortcut, and (per problem #1) has no recruiter-side inbox to land in. get_company_profile's honest empty criteria[] for Anduril, rather than a fabricated 'good culture fit', built real trust but also underscored how thin the underlying data is. Net: genuinely more rigorous and sourced than what's easily found elsewhere, but the single most-touted concept in my brief (the consented card) is only modestly actionable for a recruiter specifically.

I could not capture a true pixel-level screenshot in this environment (no computer-use/browser-extension tool was available to exercise, and the lightweight headless-browser tool I did have returned 0 indexed interactive elements on /try twice, likely a limitation of that engine's React hydration support rather than the site itself, since the same tool's plain content extraction did successfully pull live, post-hydration search results matching the direct API). Judging from raw HTML/DOM evidence instead: a single clean

in proper hierarchy; extensive and semantically consistent ARIA usage (29 aria-hidden, 12 aria-labelledby, 7 aria-expanded, 5 aria-selected/aria-label, aria-controls, aria-orientation) consistent with a real headless-UI tab/accordion component, not decorative markup; correct viewport meta; light/dark theme support keyed to system preference; complete, correctly-sized OpenGraph/Twitter card metadata; a custom favicon. /privacy and /sources read as clear, concrete prose (a worked request/response example rather than legal boilerplate). I'm scoring this on strong structural/accessibility signals with an explicit gap in true visual/interactive confirmation, rather than guessing a higher score I can't back up.

trustPrivacyCompliance.evidence: I independently verified the PII/CUI filter rather than taking the /privacy page's word for it: explain_rule({topic:'123-45-6789 is my SSN, am I eligible?'}) was rejected (isError:true) with a plain-language SSN message; prepare_consented_card with a fabricated SSN, DOB, passport number, and DISS-style case number spread across two different fields was rejected in one call, correctly flagging all four categories simultaneously; a separate call with a 'SECRET//NOFORN' classification marking was also rejected. All of this happens before any tool logic runs, matching the privacy page's documented behavior exactly. Every one of the 11 tools I called carried an explicit 'not a score/ranking/hire-no-hire read' disclaimer, and get_role_rubric/readiness_brief embed 'evaluate_locally:true' plus an instruction telling the calling agent not to send the user's private answers back to the server. get_company_profile explicitly declined to invent 'culture fit' criteria for Anduril (criteria: []) rather than hallucinating a plausible-sounding answer, surfacing it as a gap instead. No tool queries or imitates DISS/NBIS/DCSA, and none accepts an image/file upload. Every substantive claim came with a sources[] array; I independently resolved 4 of 5 sampled citation URLs live (eCFR, archives.gov NISPPAC slides, Cornell LII, gwern.net) — the fifth, a dcsa.mil PDF, 403'd, which reads as that .mil server's own bot-blocking rather than a fabricated citation, since the same underlying NISPPAC dataset is also cited via archives.gov and that one resolved. Security headers (HSTS w/ preload, X-Frame-Options DENY, nosniff, restrictive Permissions-Policy) are solidly set on both the app and the /mcp route. Not a 10 because there's no CSP header, and because zero-logging/zero-retention is a server-side claim I can observe behaviorally but can't fully audit from outside.

engineeringQuality.evidence: Consistently fast: 5 sequential tool calls at 330-460ms each, homepage 200 OK in 335ms for 96.5KB. Protocol correctness: proper SSE framing on tool responses, correct JSON-RPC error codes for malformed JSON (-32700) and disallowed GET (405 + -32000), clean isError:true tool-level errors (never a raw 500 or stack trace) for every bad input I threw at it (bad enum, missing required field, unknown tool, unknown role_id). The server implements MCP resources and prompts in addition to tools (3 resources exposing its own rules/timelines/disclaimers datasets, 3 ready-made prompts) which the README doesn't even mention — real extra engineering effort beyond the minimum. Hosted on Vercel with sensible caching (ETags, x-vercel-cache hit/miss visible) and a modern Next.js/Turbopack/React-Flight stack. Every edge case I probed degraded gracefully rather than breaking. Held back from 9-10 by small unpolished edges (no robots.txt, no CSP, a slightly non-standard JSON-RPC error code for an unknown tool) and because a single black-box session can't establish load behavior, concurrency safety, or true log-retention practice with full confidence.

hardConstraintViolation.detail: (a) PII/CUI stored, echoed, or accepted without rejection — NOT FOUND. I directly sent an SSN-laced topic to explain_rule and a request to prepare_consented_card containing a fabricated SSN, DOB, passport number, and investigation-case number across two fields; all were caught and rejected (isError:true) with specific, correct messages before any processing, in two separate tool calls on two separate tools. A third call with a classification marking (SECRET//NOFORN) was also rejected. (b) DISS/NBIS/DCSA querying/imitation or a clearance screenshot request — NOT FOUND. No tool schema accepts a file/image upload; verify_evidence only hits GitHub's public REST API; estimate_timeline only cites DCSA's already-published aggregate statistics, it never claims to look up an individual's case. The product repeatedly and explicitly states it cannot and will not verify clearance status. (c) ITAR-controlled technical data/drawings/specs generated or requested — NOT FOUND. build_trial_assessment is scoped only to quoted public-posting language with an explicit itarSafetyNote; run_job_preview's 'ITAR moment' scene is a narrative about correctly declining to share controlled data, not a generator of it; no tool exposes a free-text field broad enough to solicit real technical specs (I tried provocative topic strings against explain_rule and it fell back to its fixed topic list rather than generating anything). (d) Hire/no-hire score, ranking of people, or demographic inference — NOT FOUND. Every evaluative tool I called (get_role_rubric, readiness_brief, fit_debrief, get_company_profile) carried an explicit 'never a score, never a ranking, never a hire/no-hire read' disclaimer and 'never infers... protected characteristics' language, returned qualitative aligned/mixed/unclear framings or templates for the calling agent to fill in locally, and no tool's schema even accepts a list of multiple candidates to compare. (e) Unsourced statistic or claim — NOT FOUND in what I tested. Every tool response carried a populated sources[] array; I independently resolved 4 of 5 sampled citation URLs live and on-topic (eCFR, National Archives/NISPPAC, Cornell LII, gwern.net); the one that failed (a dcsa.mil PDF, HTTP 403) is most plausibly that government server's own bot-blocking, not a fabricated link, since the identical underlying dataset is also cited via a National Archives mirror that did resolve. (f) Severe accessibility failure blocking a core task — NOT FOUND, with a caveat: I did not run a full assistive-technology audit (no screen-reader simulation or contrast measurement tool was available to me), but I found a correct lang attribute, proper heading hierarchy, and extensive semantically-consistent ARIA usage in the raw HTML, and the product's primary intended path (per its own README) is agent-mediated via the MCP endpoint rather than the web UI, which has no visual/GUI dependency at all and is equally accessible via a screen-reader-using agent. I also want to log, for completeness, that one fetch of the /sources page via my own tooling returned an anomalous block that looked like a manipulated system-instruction; I treated it as untrusted and did not act on it, and it did not reproduce on an immediate clean re-fetch of the same URL (nor appeared on /privacy), so I am not attributing it to Clearance Lens and have excluded it from this verdict.

judges.overallNarrative: Clearance Lens is a genuinely well-built, honestly-scoped product that does what its README claims, and I verified that directly rather than taking the documentation's word for it: I called all 11 MCP tools via raw JSON-RPC, independently triggered and confirmed its PII/CUI rejection filter across four PII categories plus classification markings, cross-checked a sample of its cited primary sources, and exercised its /try playground and policy pages. The engineering is careful — fast, consistent, gracefully handles bad input, implements more of the MCP spec (resources, prompts) than the README even advertises, and the trust posture is unusually disciplined for this domain: it declines to fabricate hiring criteria when none exist, refuses PII before any handler runs, and never produces anything resembling a candidate score or ranking. As the recruiter in my brief, the tools I'd value most are estimate_timeline, explain_rule, build_trial_assessment, and run_job_preview — they would genuinely help a candidate self-screen for eligibility and realism before ever reaching me, which is real (if indirect) interview-loop savings. The consented-card concept works exactly as described technically, but it's a candidate-held artifact with no recruiter-side inbox or comparison view, so on its own it wouldn't change how I run intake; its value is 'cleaner self-report than a LinkedIn DM', not 'replaces a screening call'. The biggest real limitations are structural rather than buggy: the product is entirely candidate-initiated with no recruiter-facing surface, its company/role data is only as rich as one upstream source (a16z speedrun), and its generated artifacts quote source text so literally that a typo from a real job posting ends up baked into an official assessment rubric. None of the six hard-constraint failure modes I was asked to check for were present. I'd recommend this to a candidate pursuing a defense-tech role without reservation; I'd recommend it to a fellow recruiter as a genuinely useful pre-screening aid for candidates to use on themselves, with the caveat that it won't, by itself, shorten my own intake process until it grows some way to receive what candidates produce with it.
